answers.label: A
answers.value: i and t; ii and r; iii and s; iv and q
answers.working:
Take each feature in turn.

**i. Cytoplasm but no nucleus:** a mature **sieve tube** element keeps a thin layer of living cytoplasm but loses its nucleus; its companion cell does the nuclear work for it. The companion cell itself has a nucleus, so u is wrong here. So i matches t.

**ii. No cytoplasm and no nucleus:** a **tracheid** is a dead, lignified xylem cell with an empty lumen. So ii matches r.

**iii. More than two nuclei:** **tapetum** cells often become multinucleate (or polyploid) as they nourish the developing pollen. A synergid has a single nucleus. So iii matches s.

**iv. Haploid cell made by mitosis:** the functional megaspore divides by three rounds of mitosis to form the embryo sac, so a **synergid** is a haploid cell produced by mitosis. A pollen grain (microspore) is haploid too, but it is produced by meiosis of the microspore mother cell. So iv matches q.

The set i-t, ii-r, iii-s, iv-q is option (A). So the answer is option (A).

Place each reaction in its stage of aerobic respiration.

- ii. Dihydroxyacetone phosphate to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate happens in **glycolysis** (after fructose-1,6-bisphosphate is split), in the cytoplasm.
- i. Pyruvate to acetyl CoA is the **link reaction** in the mitochondrial matrix.
- iii. Oxaloacetate combining with acetyl CoA to form citrate is the **first step of the Krebs cycle**.
- iv. Fumarate to malate is a **late step of the Krebs cycle**, just before malate is oxidised back to oxaloacetate.

So the order is ii, i, iii, iv. So the answer is option (A).

answers.label: A
answers.working:
The **seed coat** develops from the integuments of the ovule, which are tissues of the mother plant. So the seed coat has the mother's genotype, \(ww\), whatever pollen is used. Since seed colour depends only on the seed coat, every seed from this cross is **brown**.

The **embryo**, however, comes from the zygote: a \(w\) egg from the mother fused with a \(W\) sperm from the pollen. So the embryo is \(Ww\).

The tempting choice is white seeds, because \(W\) is dominant; but the dominant allele is in the embryo, not in the maternal seed coat. Its effect will show only in the seeds borne by the next generation. So the answer is option (A).

answers.label: B
answers.working: SARS-CoV-2 is a coronavirus. Its genome is a single molecule of **single-stranded, positive-sense RNA** (about 30,000 nucleotides long), which can be read directly by the host ribosomes. RNA viruses mutate quickly because their RNA-dependent RNA polymerase copies the genome with little proofreading, which is why so many variants arose during the pandemic. So the answer is option (B).

answers.label: C
answers.value: It remains as an interstitial fluid and is never put back into circulation.
answers.working:
As blood passes through capillaries, water and small solutes filter out into the spaces between cells, forming **interstitial (tissue) fluid**. This fluid is colourless and has nearly the same minerals as plasma, so statement (A) is correct, and statement (B) describes its formation.

The excess fluid is collected by lymphatic vessels as **lymph**, which drains into the major veins and so is returned to the blood. So statement (C), which says it is never put back into circulation, is false.

Statement (D) is correct: digested fats are absorbed into the **lacteals** of the intestinal villi, which are lymph vessels.

The incorrect statement is (C). So the answer is option (C).

answers.label: D
answers.working: In a spinal reflex arc, the sensory neuron enters through the dorsal root and synapses in the spinal cord with an **interneuron**, which in turn connects to the motor neuron. These synapses and the cell bodies of interneurons lie in the **gray matter** of the spinal cord (the central, butterfly-shaped region). The white matter carries only myelinated tracts, the dorsal root ganglion holds the cell bodies of sensory neurons, and the muscle spindle is a receptor in the muscle. So the answer is option (D).

answers.label: C
answers.value: They stimulate hypothalamus to facilitate the release of the anti-diuretic hormone and increase water reabsorption.
answers.working:
When body fluid volume falls or its concentration rises, **osmoreceptors** (located in the hypothalamus) are activated. They stimulate the hypothalamus to release **ADH (vasopressin)** from the neurohypophysis. ADH acts on the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct to increase water reabsorption, so less water is lost in urine.

The other options describe different controls: ANF release is triggered by stretching of the atrial wall, mineralocorticoids come from the adrenal cortex (not the pituitary), and renin is released by the juxtaglomerular apparatus in response to a fall in glomerular blood flow or pressure. So the answer is option (C).

Here a **single gene** (one point mutation in gene X) affects **several unrelated traits**: breathing, blood pressure and fertility. A single gene influencing multiple phenotypic traits is called **pleiotropy** (phenylketonuria is the textbook example).

Linkage concerns two or more genes inherited together, and partial or incomplete dominance describes how two alleles of one gene combine to affect a single trait. None of these explains many traits from one mutation. So the answer is option (D).

answers.label: B
answers.working:
With independent assortment, treat each gene separately and multiply.

- \(Pp \times pp\): probability of \(pp\) is \(\frac{1}{2}\).
- \(QQ \times qq\): every offspring gets \(Q\) from one parent and \(q\) from the other, so all are \(Qq\). The probability of \(QQ\) is \(0\).
- \(Rr \times Rr\): probability of \(Rr\) is \(\frac{1}{2}\).
- \(SS \times SS\): probability of \(SS\) is \(1\).

Probability of \(ppQQRrSS = \frac{1}{2} \times 0 \times \frac{1}{2} \times 1 = 0\), so out of 400 progeny the expected number is \(400 \times 0 = 0\). The \(qq\) parent can never pass on a \(Q\) allele. So the answer is option (B).

**Platyhelminthes** (flatworms such as tapeworm and liver fluke) are bilaterally symmetrical and triploblastic, but have **no body cavity**: the space between the body wall and the gut is filled with mesoderm. So they are acoelomate.

Mollusca, Arthropoda and Hemichordata are also bilateral and triploblastic, but all of them are **coelomates** (true body cavity), so they do not fit. So the answer is option (A).

answers.label: A
answers.working:
Net primary productivity depends mainly on sunlight, warmth, water and nutrients.

- **Tropical rainforest (P):** warm, wet and sunny all year, so it has the highest NPP of any land biome (about 2000 g per square metre per year).
- **Coastal zone (S):** nutrient-rich waters (estuaries, continental shelf, upwelling) give a high productivity, the highest among marine zones but below rainforests.
- **Tundra (Q):** very cold, with a short growing season, so NPP is low.
- **Desert (R):** water is the limiting factor almost all the time, so NPP is the lowest.

The descending order is \(P > S > Q > R\). So the answer is option (A).
answers.flag: Tundra vs desert NPP are close in standard tables (roughly 140 vs 90 g/m2/yr), but tundra is still higher; only option A places P first and R last with S second, so the choice is clear.

answers.label: C
answers.working:
Non-tasters are homozygous recessive, so their frequency is \(q^2\).

\(q^2 = 0.09\), so \(q = \sqrt{0.09} = 0.3\).

Since \(p + q = 1\), the dominant allele frequency is \(p = 1 - 0.3 = 0.7\).

The question asks for the dominant and recessive allele frequencies in that order: 0.7 and 0.3. Option (B) gives the same numbers in the wrong order. So the answer is option (C).

answers.label: A
answers.value: Denaturation step in PCR substitutes for the replication fork and Taq polymerase extends DNA only in the 5' to 3' direction.
answers.working:
In a cell, the two strands are opened gradually at a moving **replication fork**. Because DNA polymerase can add nucleotides only in the 5' to 3' direction, one strand (the lagging strand) must be made in short Okazaki fragments as the fork keeps opening.

In PCR there is no moving fork. Heating (**denaturation**) separates the two strands completely, so each whole strand is available as a template at once. A primer anneals to each strand and **Taq polymerase** extends it continuously in the 5' to 3' direction to the end of the template. Hence no discontinuous synthesis is needed.

Options (B) and (D) are wrong because no replication fork forms in PCR, and Taq has no ligase activity; option (C) is wrong because no DNA polymerase synthesises in the 3' to 5' direction. So the answer is option (A).

answers.label: D
answers.value: ETC moves \(\mathrm{H^+}\) from MM up into IMS; the ATP synthase head sits on the MM side, \(\mathrm{H^+}\) passes through ATP synthase from IMS down into MM, and ADP becomes ATP on the MM side
answers.working:
According to the **chemiosmotic hypothesis**, the complexes of the electron transport chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane pump \(\mathrm{H^+}\) **from the matrix into the intermembrane space**. This builds a high \(\mathrm{H^+}\) concentration in the intermembrane space.

The protons then flow back **down their gradient, from the intermembrane space into the matrix**, through the \(\mathrm{F_0}\) channel of ATP synthase. The \(\mathrm{F_1}\) head (the knob where ADP and \(\mathrm{P_i}\) join to form ATP) projects **into the matrix**, so ATP is made on the matrix side.

Only figure (D) shows all three: ETC pumping from MM to IMS, \(\mathrm{H^+}\) returning from IMS to MM through ATP synthase, and the head with ADP to ATP on the MM side. Figure (A) has the right proton flow but puts the head and ATP formation in the IMS. So the answer is option (D).

answers.label: B
answers.working:
At **metaphase** the chromosomes are lined up with their centromeres on the equatorial (metaphase) plate, so X is about zero. In **early metaphase** (prometaphase) chromosomes are still moving towards the plate, so X is small.

In **anaphase** the sister chromatids separate and their centromeres are pulled towards opposite poles, centromere first. X increases steadily as anaphase proceeds, so it is small in early anaphase and greatest in **late anaphase**, when the chromatids have reached the poles.

So the stage with the highest average X is late anaphase. So the answer is option (B).
